data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001's silence-completion signature has no causal mechanism linking better-than-chance accuracy on checklist-silent items to genuine reliability rather than to a shared latent prior. On items where the checklist is silent, panelists may systematically infer the correct answer because the silent items covary with a background regularity the checklist's authors relied upon but did not codify; the panel then tracks correctness without exercising any competence the checklist did not already encode. The target's own countercondition concedes that systematic guessing could be bias, not competence, but its main claim still treats better-than-chance accuracy as the signature of genuine reliability. Without a mechanism that separates latent-prior exploitation from externalized competence, silence-completion collapses back into a tracking artifact and cannot distinguish genuine reliability gain within a single evaluation.
